extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (practitioners and scholars of patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal principles and tests governing patent assignments, licenses, estoppel, surrender/reissue effects, and the basics of infringement—how instruments are construed, what rights pass, and when licensees are estopped from challenging validity. Focused on procedural and substantive consequences for parties' rights and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of surrender and reissue on assignees' rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute authorizing surrender and reissue of a patent on account of a defective specification expressly 'saves the rights of assignees in the patent' and, strictly, an assignee should be a party to the surrender; but if the surrender is made by the patentee the assignments made before the surrender are not vacated and the interests of assignees remain the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory clause quoted: rights of assignees are preserved; practical note that assignee ought to be party to surrender but absence of assignee does not necessarily void prior assignments; cases cited (e.g., Woodworth v. Stone) support that assignments prior to surrender survive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissued patent treated as same patent and relates back to original term
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent has been surrendered and new letters taken out with an amended specification, the reissued patent has generally been considered to operate, except as to suits for violations committed before the amendment, from the commencement of the original term; the amendment is not because the former patent was utterly void but because it was defective or doubtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to amended writs and judgments: amended matter treated as if originally in them. Consequence: new letters relate back to original issue date for many purposes and do not create a new independent term running from reissue date; cannot lawfully include a new invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoveries under original patent as evidence after reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: Recoveries under the original patent are evidence after issuance of new letters and new specification to strengthen the plaintiff's title so as to obtain an injunction, treating the patent as one and the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior successful suits under original letters can be used post-reissue to support equitable relief; cited cases (Orr v. Littlefield, Orr v. Badger) illustrate the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee's rights with respect to extensions and renewals
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee or grantee under the original patent does not acquire any right under an extended patent (pursuant to §18 of the Act of 1836) unless such right is expressly conveyed to him by the patentee; however, assignees who were in the use of a patented machine at time of renewal may have rights to use under renewal clause extending benefit to assignees to extent of their interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes ordinary assignments from rights conferred by statutory renewals/extensions; explicit conveyance required to pass rights arising from later extension unless licensee/assignee was in use and statute clause applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file a statutory disclaimer (Act of 1837 §7 and §9)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a disclaimer is to be filed under the 7th and 9th sections of the Act of 1837, an assignee of the whole patent will be the proper party to file it; if the patent has been previously assigned in part, the disclaimer will not operate to the benefit of such a partial assignee in any suit by him unless he joined in the disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule about standing to disclaim: whole-patent assignee can file; partial assignees must join to benefit in subsequent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and test for assignment versus license
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment is a grant in writing of the whole or part of the exclusive right vested in the patentee by the patent (either undivided or territorial). A license grants the right to make, use, and sell the thing patented but does not confer an interest in the patent. The test is whether the instrument vests in the grantee the exclusive right (and the right to grant that right to others); if so, it is an assignment; if it merely grants a non-exclusive right to make/use/sell, it is a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory recording consequences flow from this test. Example: grant of 'right and privilege of making, using, and selling' with provisos that reserve patentee's ability to make/vend was held to be a license (not recordable). Instruments should be examined for language granting exclusivity and power to grant to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording requirement hinges on exclusive right + right to grant others
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statute, a grant requires recording only if it embraces the exclusive right of making and using and includes the right to grant to others to make and use the thing patented; mere licenses are not required to be recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions (e.g., Brooks v. Byam) support that exclusive authority without power to grant to others may still be treated as a license for statutory purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of instruments: intent, reservations, and indicia of license
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where language purports to confer an exclusive right, if the tenor of the whole instrument shows the parties intended it to operate as a license rather than an assignment, courts will so construe it. Provisos terminating the grant or reservation of a rent or percentage on gross sales (rather than an interest in profits) are indicia of a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look to entire instrument for intent; reservations and covenant structure (rent/percentage) suggest license. Conversely, power to grant to others points toward assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignability and apportionability of licenses depend on terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a license is assignable depends on its terms; a mere license to the party without mentioning his assigns confers a personal right not transmissible. The use of the word 'assigns' does not necessarily make a license assignable when the whole instrument indicates a personal privilege. Apportionability (splitting one license into multiple parts each assignable) is more questionable and requires clear language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., the friction-matches license) indicate courts construe conveyances according to their terms and object; a license may be transmissible but not apportionable unless the contract clearly contemplates subdivision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indivisibility of certain granted privileges (practical example)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the language and object of a grant show the license or privilege was intended as an entirety (e.g., 'one right, embracing one person'), the court may hold it incapable of being split into distinct rights assignable in severalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual construction is required; courts consider practical consequences and potential fraud/abuse to the patentee when deciding whether to permit subdivision of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel by license recitals, admissions, and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The taking of a naked license or permission to work under a patent does not, without recitals or covenants, estop the licensee from denying validity; but if the deed contains recitals or admissions of validity or the licensee admits the process is patented or works under and pays under the license, he may be estopped from denying validity or infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel arises from admissions in the deed, payments made, continued claim under the deed, or other conduct; if patentee joins issue rather than pleads estoppel, deed may be evidentiary but not conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to recover payments and failure of consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee who has paid an annuity for the benefit of a license which later turns out to be void may not recover the money paid if he has had the benefit; however, if the patent is shown to be invalid before a payment becomes due and the license deed contains no admission of validity, the licensee may plead failure of consideration or the invalidity as a defense to an action for payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish payments made after enjoyment (no recovery) from payments not yet due when invalidity can be interposed; look to admissions in deed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee who repudiates the contract risks becoming a trespasser
rubrics_metrics.description: If a licensee repudiates the license and asserts the right to use the alleged invention because it is not new, he foregoes the benefits of the license and becomes a trespasser; in that event solemn admissions under hand and seal may be used against him as an estoppel unless he can show deception or misleading conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity requires a licensee to do everything in his power to perform the contract before alleging patentee's non-performance; failure to perform may preclude reliance on the license as a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and test of infringement: substance over form
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement occurs whenever a party avails himself of the invention of the patentee without such variation as will constitute a new discovery; stated another way, an infringement is a copy made after and agreeing with the principle laid down in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts focus on whether the defendant's device or process in reality, in substance and effect, avails itself of the patentee's invention—immaterial variations in form do not avoid infringement. Compare plaintiff's and defendant's specifications and consider principle, substance, and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of infringement is a question of fact for the jury (compare specifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether what has been done by defendants amounts to such an infringement is often a question of fact for the jury: they must compare the plaintiff's specification with the defendant's and decide whether there is a substantial variation or whether the defendant has followed the plaintiff's invention with only immaterial changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial instructions emphasize comparing specifications and the 'reality' of whether the defendant has availed himself of plaintiff's invention; cited case law shows jury's role in resolving the factual issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misjoinder of plaintiffs in infringement suits generally does not defeat injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A misjoinder of parties as plaintiffs in this kind of application would be an objection in abatement at law and probably could not be objected to in equity such as to defeat a prayer for an injunction; final judgments will be entered for those who appear to have some right and interest to be protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical litigation point: misjoinder typically will not bar injunctive relief; courts will protect those with proven interests and limit relief accordingly.
